title: After Sitting Idle for Decades, This Rare 427-Powered Caprice Is Back on the Streets

body_markdown:
In the 1960s, America’s automakers offered all kinds of cars with performance-oriented V-8s. Ford let buyers check a box to get a 428 Cobra Jet in the sporty Torino and Cobra, but also in the Fairlane. Dodge and Plymouth built a handful of four-doors and wagons with the legendary 426 Hemi. Like Ford and Mopar, Chevrolet let buyers put its rowdiest V-8s of the ‘60s into plenty of rides you might not expect, like this well-optioned 1966 Caprice that’s powered by a 425-horsepower, solid-lifter, L72 427.


Scott Jones at Corvette Shop in Costa Mesa, California, rebuilt the engine and transmission. The block wasn’t decked, so the original stampings on the deck surface were left intact.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


We met Kelly Holcomb, who just wrapped up the final few bits and bobs of the Caprice’s restoration, near Long Beach. He purchased this car in 2015, planning to restore it to its original condition and get it on the road once more. “I’ve known about the car for, I would say, probably close to 30 years,” Holcomb explained. Bob McKray, an enigne builder in south Orange County, had owned it since the mid-‘80s. McKray’s neighbor bought the car new in 1965 from Jim Robertson Chevrolet in San Clemente, California. Even though McKray was just a child then, he remembered when the car arrived on their block. By the time he got it, the car was rough on the edges and in need of repair.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


McKray stored the car at drag racer Art Chrisman’s shop, and he had hoped to restore it at some point. Initially, Holcomb thought it was just a regular old B-body. Its engine was out, stored on site but out of view, and its fender emblems were gone, making way for the fenders to get primed. He soon came to understand how rare the car was. In 1966, Chevy only built 1856 full-size cars—Biscayne, Bel Air, Impala, and Caprice—with the brand’s most powerful 427. The majority went to racers who wanted to put the engine to the test on the track.


Westminster Auto Body handled the Caprice’s paint and bodywork.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Chevy’s L72 427 big-block came with a solid-lifter cam, requiring more frequent maintenance than its hydraulic-lifter counterparts at the time. Hydraulic lifters don’t have to be lashed as often and offer smoother, quieter operation, but a solid-lifter valvetrain offers more valve lift and allows for more air to get into and out of the combustion chamber to make more power. The engine was only available with a four-speed manual and was not offered with air conditioning. Most buyers opting for such a racy engine would have opted for the lightweight Biscayne two-door post or the flashier Impala Super Sport. As such, very few Caprices left the factory with an L72. “The different records say anywhere from eight to 20 of those cars were built,” said Holcomb. The engine alone makes the car special. The fact that it’s a Caprice makes it even more so. If you’re really into the weeds, this one was ordered without a vinyl top, which would have been standard on the Caprice coupe’s formal roof in 1966. The black-on-black combo with a vinyl top delete appears to make it a one-of-one 1966 L72.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


When Holcomb bought the Caprice more than 10 years ago, it was apart, but complete. “The car retained the original motor and transmission,” Holcomb said, “all the original parts that bolt onto the engine were there. They were in pieces, but they were there.” The factory cast-iron exhaust manifolds had been removed and replaced by tubular headers before they had driven long enough to burn off the orange engine paint overspray. “They put headers on it immediately, and then drove it that way, drag raced it, took it to Orange County (International Raceway) all the time, Holcomb told us, “I mean, it’s a fast car with that motor in it.” In addition to the factory parts that came with the car, McKray had a stack of past state vehicle registrations, the Protect-O-Plate warranty card, and some photos of the car taken by late Hot Rod magazine staffers Gray Baskerville and Pad Ganahl, who had both hoped to chart the car’s restoration in the ’90s. They also appreciated this rare machine.


This is what the Caprice looked like for decades. Without a close look at the interior or engine bay, it would have been easy to overlook its rarity.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


The factory cast iron exhaust manifolds were removed just a week or two after the car was purchased in favor of tubular headers. They still had Chevy orange overspray from the engine’s factory paint job and served as a template for the engine’s current paint job.


We’ve covered the value disparity between the[collector favorite Impala and the lesser-known big-block variants of the Caprice](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/1966-70-chevy-caprice-lagging-behind-the-impala/) . The fact that these big coupes were so rarely equipped with such race-bred engines should make them a big draw, yet it’s the Impala Super Sport that collectors clamor for. None of that matters to Holcomb, who appreciates that a car like this was special ordered and so unique. “I had to have this car because of the rarity,” Holcomb said. When the time came in 2015 that McKray was ready to sell it, he knew he had a ready buyer. Holcomb explained, “He \[McKray\] said, ‘There’s only one guy I know who’s going to restore it the way it needs to be restored.'” There are a handful of parts that are unique to L72 B-bodies. “Luckily, most of them were there,” said Holcomb. “The air cleaner only came on that car; the power steering only came on that car; the tachometer only came on that car.”


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


It’s not too much of a stretch to label this full-size luxury sedan as a sleeper. The 1966 Caprice was described in contemporary sales literature as “Chevrolet’s regal new series, as elegant as the high-priced cars but at Chevrolet prices.” It’s definitely not what you’d expect to find at your local dragstrip. The average driver at a stoplight next to a new ’66 Caprice wouldn’t assume it had a four-speed and a solid-lifter 427 ready to rip.


Holcomb plans to drive his Caprice on weekends and appreciates the contrast of a well-appointed luxury cruiser fitted with such a rowdy engine. “I want to enjoy it,” he said. “It’s a great driving car. I drove it from Newport Beach, no problem.” It’s practically the perfect classic car for coastal Southern California cruising, where mild temperatures make the lack of air conditioning a non-issue. Finally, decades after he discovered the rare coupe, and decades after its engine was removed and it sat in storage, it’s back prowling the streets of Orange County. “It was a labor of love, because it was a lot of work to get back to that condition,” said Holcomb. “It was worth it.”
